description:
Meet Team Asterea, a two-person computer engineering team competing in the NASA Space Apps Challenge in Nablus.

As engineering students, we use our background in software and systems design to rapidly build solutions for space and Earth challenges. Representing Nablus globally, we prove that small teams can tackle complex problems with agile, high-performance code.

Team Asterea is ready to reach for the cosmos, one line of code at a time.
summary:
MarsNAV is a prototype platform for exploring Mars and coordinating a simulated astronaut mission. Its desktop control center displays Mars terrain and astronaut status, while a connected phone provides an immersive, first-person exploration view with on-screen navigation guidance. Mission control can review route options and assign a destination, including a simulated emergency station.

The project combines NASA and USGS resources—including global elevation data, detailed Jezero terrain, and weather observations from the Perseverance rover—with physics-informed estimates for distance, slope, travel time, wind, and route difficulty. It distinguishes measured environmental data from simulated astronaut systems and mission scenarios.

MarsNAV addresses the challenge of making planetary data useful for exploration and decision-making: it connects terrain, environmental context, navigation, and human coordination in one interactive experience. This matters because future exploration will depend on helping crews understand unfamiliar landscapes, communicate their needs, and choose safer routes.
details:
MarsNAV is an interactive Mars exploration and mission-coordination prototype. A desktop browser provides the mission-control view, while a connected smartphone acts as the astronaut interface. The control center can monitor a simulated astronaut’s location and status, respond to requests, and assign destinations. On the phone, the astronaut can explore a Mars surface view and follow an on-screen navigation arrow.

How it works

The app brings together Mars terrain and environmental information with route-planning tools. It can compare routes using three objectives: shortest distance, gentlest terrain, and least estimated mechanical work. The calculations use terrain and weather inputs to estimate factors such as slope, distance, travel time, and wind effects. NASA and USGS resources include global elevation data, detailed terrain for part of Jezero crater, and Perseverance MEDA weather observations.

Benefits and intended impact

MarsNAV makes scientific data easier to explore and connects it to mission decisions in a shared interface. Its goal is to demonstrate how astronauts and mission control could understand terrain, coordinate destinations, and communicate during exploration. It is an educational prototype—not a certified navigation or life-support system. Environmental measurements are distinguished from simulated astronaut status and mission scenarios.

Tools, hardware, and creative approach

The project uses React and TypeScript for the web interface, Three.js for 3D visuals, Vite for development, and a Node.js/Express API server. It is designed to run in a desktop browser and on a smartphone; no special hardware is required. Its creative element is the combination of a dual-screen mission-control experience, Mars terrain data, physics-informed route comparisons, and game-style astronaut guidance.

Factors considered

Development considered data sources and resolution, scientific uncertainty, device compatibility, readable astronaut controls, privacy around phone sensors, and the need to clearly separate measured data from simulations
